subject: Physics
chapter: Chapter 11: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
central_question: How do experiments show that radiation and matter can each display both particle-like and wave-like behaviour?
in_scope_units: Introduction to cathode rays, the universal electron, specific charge and quantisation of electric charge.
Electron emission, work function and thermionic, field and photoelectric emission.
Discovery of the photoelectric effect through the observations of Hertz, Hallwachs and Lenard.
Experimental arrangement for studying photoelectric current.
Effect of incident-light intensity on photocurrent and saturation current.
Effect of collector potential on photocurrent, stopping potential and maximum kinetic energy.
Effect of radiation frequency on stopping potential, threshold frequency and instantaneous emission.
Failure of the classical wave theory to explain the observed photoelectric effect.
Einstein’s photoelectric equation and the quantum or photon explanation of radiation.
Particle nature of light, photon energy, momentum and conservation principles.
Wave nature of matter, de Broglie hypothesis and de Broglie wavelength.
Comparison of measurable matter waves for microscopic particles with unobservably small wavelengths for macroscopic objects.
banned_topics: Detailed Bohr atomic model and hydrogen energy levels, which belong to Chapter 12: Atoms.
Detailed Compton-scattering derivation, which is mentioned as supporting evidence but is not developed in this chapter.
Quantum-mechanical wave functions, uncertainty principle and Schrödinger equation, which are beyond the supplied chapter.

known_pitfalls.claim: Increasing light intensity increases the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons.
known_pitfalls.correction: For fixed frequency and emitter material, intensity increases photocurrent and saturation current but does not change stopping potential or maximum kinetic energy.

known_pitfalls.claim: Any sufficiently intense light can produce photoelectric emission from a metal.
known_pitfalls.correction: No emission occurs below the metal’s threshold frequency, however large the intensity or exposure time.

known_pitfalls.claim: All electrons emitted from a metal have the same kinetic energy.
known_pitfalls.correction: Photoelectrons have a distribution of kinetic energies; the stopping potential corresponds to the most energetic electrons.

known_pitfalls.claim: A larger object has an easily observable de Broglie wavelength if it moves fast.
known_pitfalls.correction: Because λ = h/p, macroscopic momenta make de Broglie wavelengths extremely small and experimentally unobservable.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Example 11.1 to calculate photon energy and photon rate from laser frequency and power.
Use NCERT Example 11.2 to connect work function, threshold frequency, stopping potential and wavelength.
Apply NCERT Exercise 11.2 to calculate maximum kinetic energy, stopping potential and maximum photoelectron speed.
Use NCERT Exercise 11.5 to obtain Planck’s constant from the slope of the stopping-potential versus frequency graph.
Finish with NCERT Example 11.3 or Exercise 11.10 to compare de Broglie wavelengths of microscopic and macroscopic objects.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter EXERCISES are numbered 11.1 to 11.11 and cover X-ray limits, photoelectric calculations, photon energy and momentum, Planck’s constant, work function and de Broglie wavelength.
